title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
claim: Under distribution shift, different input regions need different update actions (learn, keep, or forget), so one global reset is wrong.
layout: single panel, time on x-axis, bracketed regions labeled (a)-(d) at right
description: A single scatter plot of a synthetic univariate stream. Time runs along the x-axis and feature value along the y-axis. Blue circles are Class 0 and red crosses are Class 1. A legend in the top left also lists a gray dashed vertical line as the drift moment, which splits the plot into pre-drift (left) and post-drift (right) halves. Four black brackets on the right edge mark feature-value bands. (a) Updating is the top band, where red crosses appear only after the drift. (b) Stable is the upper-middle band with blue circles both before and after. (c) (Active) Forgetting is the lower-middle band, where red crosses before the drift are replaced by blue circles after it. (d) Stable is the bottom band with red crosses both before and after. The eye goes first to the dense red and blue clusters, then to the dashed line and the bracket labels.
caption: illustrates why feature subspaces must be taken into account when learning in settings with concept drift. Given a univariate stream with a single drift moment (dashed line) and assuming a model was trained on data prior to the drift, different actions need to be taken to update the model on the post-drift data, depending on the location in the feature space. Subspace (a) is entirely new, so the optimal action is to learn in that new region. Subspaces (b) and (d) are stable (i.e., no drift), so no action needs to be taken (the model still classifies instances in those regions correctly). Subspace (c) however, requires that the model actively forgets instances from the past before learning on instances from the current time context (i.e., the pre-drift context conflicts with the post-drift context).
abstract: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous. Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.
